newsitem.title: USA: MGM buying film libary, studio for $573 million.
newsitem.headline: MGM buying film libary, studio for $573 million.

text.p: Hollywood studio Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Inc. Monday announced plans to acquire Metromedia International Group Inc.'s entertainment group and film library for $573 million in cash.

The deal, which had been expected for over a week, would expand MGM's catalogue to more than 3,800 films that it can market to basic television and home video as well as emerging formats in satellite TV, digital video disks and computer CD-ROMs.
"This acquisition more than doubles the size of MGM's library, giving it the added distinction of being the largest modern film library in the world," MGM Chairman Frank Mancuso said in a statement.
Metromedia is shedding assets that financial analysts and investors complained have soaked up capital needed for expanding its telecommunications businesses in eastern Europe.
Since buying two film production companies last year, Metromedia's stock has fallen from about $16.50 a share to $8.75 Monday.

Under the deal, MGM will buy Atlanta-based Metromedia's 2,200-title film and television library and the production and distribution activities of its entertainment group, including Orion Pictures Corp., Goldwyn Entertainment Co. and Motion Picture Corp. of America, the companies said.

Under the deal, Metromedia's cable television systems will get first crack at MGM movies available in countries where Metromedia operates cable TV networks, including the Metromedia Entertainment Network in Eastern Europe.
In addition to the library, MGM will acquire 12 completed movies and five direct-to-video features for future release.
The companies said the transaction does not include Metromedia's Landmark Theatre Group, with 138 screens at 50 locations in the United States. But analysts said Metromedia could easily find a buyer.
MGM, bought by billionaire Kirk Kerkorian and Australian media conglomerate Seven Network Ltd. for $1.3 billion last fall, has been trying to bolster its library and boost revenues.

Added to MGM's current library, which includes classic films like "Midnight Cowboy" and the James Bond movies, will be popular hits such as Oscar winners "Dances With Wolves" and "The Silence of the Lambs." MGM's existing library is already tied to licensing deals well past the year 2000.
The films also give MGM a major asset with a concrete value if it decides to sell stock to the public, which Mancuso has said he may do.
Under the deal, Metromedia will repay $200 million to $300 of debt, financial analysts said.

"This transaction will provide our company with the opportunity to focus our efforts on the expansion of our telecommunications systems in Eastern Europe and the Far East," Metromedia Chairman John Kluge said in a statement.
Metromedia owns cable television outlets, paging services, radio and telephone operations in Russia, Georgia, Belarus and several other countries in the former Russian Republic.

Kluge entered the entertainment business about 10 years ago when Metromedia bought Orion. In 1996, it acquired Motion Picture Corp. for about $22 million and Goldwyn for about $44 million in Metromedia stock.

It had planned to use the movie division to provide U.S. programming for its cable TV systems in Europe. Many market experts, however, questioned how quickly it could exploit that opportunity, and Metromedia has come under growing pressure on Wall Street for not having a clear strategy in this arena.
The deal, which is subject to approval by both companies' stockholders, is expected to close this summer.
In addition to movies, MGM has a 4,500-title home video library and a television library and owns MGM Pictures, United Artists Pictures, MGM Music and MGM Interactive.
Metromedia stock fell 56.25 cents to $8.75 on the American Stock Exchange.
